name: EcoFlow 220W Bifacial Solar Panel
summary: A 220W folding panel with a bifacial rear, MC4 output and a kickstand case; the best all-round panel for most 500Wh–2kWh power stations, whatever the brand.
verdict:
The EcoFlow 220W Bifacial is the best all-round folding panel for most power station owners, whatever brand of station you have. It is big enough to matter, small enough for one person to set up, and it uses the universal MC4 connector.

**Bifacial is a bonus, not the headline.** EcoFlow rates the front at 220W and the rear at 155W. The rear only earns its keep when light bounces back off the ground: sand, snow, concrete or a white tarp help, while dark soil and grass add little. Size your system on the 220W front and treat anything extra as found energy.

**Do the sun-hour math.** A clear summer day gives about 5 peak sun hours. At roughly 75% of rating after heat and angle losses, 220W × 5 × 0.75 is about 825Wh, enough to put back most of a 1kWh battery such as the [EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus](/gear/ecoflow-delta-3-plus/). In winter, with 2–3 sun hours, expect about half that. The [power station runtime calculator](/tools/power-station-runtime-calculator/) shows what that energy will run.

**Check voltage before you chain two.** The spec sheet lists 21.8V open-circuit, so two in series sit near 44V. That suits most mid-size stations, but compare it with your station's [MPPT](/glossary/mppt/) input range first. At 20.9 lb with an IP68 rating, it handles a wet lawn and repeated setup and teardown.

Owners praise the kickstand case, which makes aiming at the sun quick, and the build quality. The main complaint is bulk: folded, it is a large, heavy slab to store. It is the top pick in our [best portable solar panel](/best-portable-solar-panel/) roundup; for more input from one panel, see the [EcoFlow 400W](/gear/ecoflow-400w-portable-solar-panel/).

faqs.q: How much can the EcoFlow 220W Bifacial charge in a day?
faqs.a: About 800Wh on a clear summer day. With roughly 5 peak sun hours and 75% real-world efficiency, 220W × 5 × 0.75 is about 825Wh. Light reflected onto the rear can add more over sand, snow or concrete. In winter, or under broken cloud, plan on roughly 300–500Wh instead.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the EcoFlow 220W Bifacial and the EcoFlow 400W panel?
faqs.a: Size and voltage. The 220W weighs 20.9 lb, runs at 21.8V open-circuit and suits almost any station. The 400W weighs 35.3 lb and runs at 48V open-circuit, so it can exceed the input limit of small stations. Choose the 400W only for a 1–2kWh station that accepts that voltage.

name: Jackery SolarSaga 100W
summary: Jackery’s 100W folding briefcase panel with kickstands and USB ports; the plug-and-play match for small Jackery Explorer stations, and one half of a pair for bigger ones.
verdict:
If you own a Jackery Explorer, the SolarSaga 100W is the easiest panel to get right. Jackery designs its cables for its own stations, so there is little to work out beyond unfolding it and pointing it at the sun.

**Match it to a small station.** One 100W panel suits stations of a few hundred watt-hours, like the [Jackery Explorer 300 Plus](/gear/jackery-explorer-300-plus/) or [Explorer 240 v2](/gear/jackery-explorer-240-v2/). On a clear summer day with about 5 peak sun hours, 100W × 5 × 0.75 is roughly 375Wh, close to a full refill for those. Against a 1kWh-plus Explorer, it puts back about a third of a charge, so plan on two.

**The connector matters.** Output is Jackery's DC8020 plug, with an adapter for older DC7909 inputs. That is plug-and-play on Explorers but needs an adapter cable on other brands. The panel also carries USB ports for charging a phone straight off the panel, handy when the station is already full.

**Built to carry.** At 9.1 lb it folds in half like a briefcase, with a handle and kickstands on the back. The spec sheet lists an IP65 rating, which covers rain and splashes but not standing water, so do not leave it lying in a puddle.

Owners like how light it is and how quickly it sets up. The main complaint is cost per watt, since generic MC4 panels deliver more watts for the money. See the [best portable solar panel](/best-portable-solar-panel/) roundup and the [best Jackery power station](/best-jackery-power-station/) guide, or step up to the [SolarSaga 200W](/gear/jackery-solarsaga-200w/).

name: Anker SOLIX PS100
amazonQuery: Anker SOLIX PS100 portable solar panel
summary: A compact 100W folding panel with an adjustable kickstand and an IP67 rating; the natural partner for smaller Anker SOLIX stations and a solid 100W panel for most others.
verdict:
The Anker SOLIX PS100 is a compact, well-made 100W panel that makes the most sense next to a smaller Anker SOLIX station. It folds small, sets up fast and is built to survive weather.

**Pair it with a small battery.** A 100W panel is a good match for stations of roughly 300–800Wh, such as the [Anker SOLIX C300X](/gear/anker-solix-c300x/) or [C800 Plus](/gear/anker-solix-c800-plus/). On a clear summer day, 100W × 5 sun hours × 0.75 is about 375Wh, more than enough to refill a C300X-class station. Against a 1kWh-plus battery like the [SOLIX C1000](/gear/anker-solix-c1000/), think of it as one panel in a pair.

**Angle is free watts.** Anker builds in an adjustable kickstand, so you can tilt the panel toward a low winter sun instead of laying it flat. Anker lists monocrystalline cells at up to 23% efficiency and an IP67 rating, which means it shrugs off rain and dust better than most fabric folders.

**Check the cable before you buy.** Anker has sold several revisions and bundles under the PS100 name, and the output plug and included adapters vary by listing. If your station is not an Anker, confirm the listing includes a cable for your station's input, or budget for one.

Owners like the compact fold and the solid kickstand. The common complaint is confusion over which cables come in the box. It features in our [best portable solar panel](/best-portable-solar-panel/) roundup and the [best Anker SOLIX power station](/best-anker-solix-power-station/) guide.

The PS100 carries a higher IP67 rating and pairs with Anker SOLIX stations; the SolarSaga uses Jackery’s DC8020 plug and pairs with Explorers. Buy the one that matches your station.

name: BLUETTI PV200
summary: A 200W folding panel with 23.4%-efficient cells and standard MC4 output, so it charges almost any power station; a strong match for 500Wh–1kWh batteries.
verdict:
The BLUETTI PV200 is a solid 200W folding panel, and its standard MC4 output means it works with almost any power station, not just BLUETTI's own.

**200W is where a panel starts to move a big battery.** On a clear summer day with about 5 peak sun hours, 200W × 5 × 0.75 is roughly 750Wh. That refills a small station like the [BLUETTI EB3A](/gear/bluetti-eb3a/) with room to spare and puts back most of a 1kWh battery such as the [BLUETTI Elite 100 V2](/gear/bluetti-elite-100-v2/). BLUETTI lists monocrystalline cells at 23.4% efficiency, among the higher figures for a folding panel.

**MC4 makes it universal.** Most stations ship with an MC4 adapter, so the PV200 plugs into EcoFlow, Jackery, Anker and BLUETTI stations alike. If you wire two in series for 400W, add their open-circuit voltages and compare the total with your station's [MPPT](/glossary/mppt/) input limit before you connect them.

**Plan for the footprint.** It weighs 16.1 lb and unfolds into a long strip that needs a patch of lawn, a truck bed or a picnic table. Kickstands on the back let you angle it toward the sun, and BLUETTI rates it IP65 for rain and splashes.

Owners report steady output and like the MC4 flexibility. The usual complaints are the large unfolded size and kickstands that can feel flimsy in wind. It is in our [best portable solar panel](/best-portable-solar-panel/) roundup; compare it with the [EcoFlow 220W Bifacial](/gear/ecoflow-220w-bifacial-portable-solar-panel/).

name: EcoFlow 400W Portable Solar Panel
summary: One 400W folding panel with a 48V output and a kickstand case; it can refill a 1–2kWh power station in a single sunny day, if the station accepts the voltage.
verdict:
The EcoFlow 400W is the panel to buy when you want to refill a large power station in one day without wiring together a stack of smaller panels. It is one panel, one cable and a lot of watts, with weight and voltage as the trade-offs.

**The math for big batteries.** On a clear summer day with about 5 peak sun hours, 400W × 5 × 0.75 is about 1,500Wh. That is most of a 2kWh battery like the [EcoFlow Delta 2 Max](/gear/ecoflow-delta-2-max/), or a full refill for a 1kWh [Delta 3 Plus](/gear/ecoflow-delta-3-plus/). For a [solar generator](/glossary/solar-generator/) setup meant to ride out a multi-day outage, that is the number that matters.

**Check the 48V open-circuit voltage.** EcoFlow lists 48V Voc, more than twice the roughly 22V of a 100W–220W panel. Large stations handle it easily, but small ones with a low input voltage limit cannot. Read your station's [MPPT](/glossary/mppt/) input range before you buy, and skip this panel for anything under about 1kWh.

**It is a two-hand job.** The spec sheet lists 35.3 lb, and unfolded it covers a lot of ground. The carry case flips out into a kickstand, and the IP68 rating means rain will not hurt it, but wind can catch it, so weigh down the case.

Owners praise how fast it refills a Delta-class station on a sunny day. The main complaints are the weight and the space it needs unfolded. It is in the [best portable solar panel](/best-portable-solar-panel/) roundup; most people with a mid-size station are better served by the [EcoFlow 220W Bifacial](/gear/ecoflow-220w-bifacial-portable-solar-panel/).

name: Renogy 100W Solar Suitcase
amazonQuery: Renogy 100W foldable solar suitcase with charge controller
summary: A rigid 100W glass-and-aluminum suitcase with a built-in charge controller and battery clips; made for charging 12V RV, marine and van batteries directly, not power stations.
verdict:
The Renogy 100W suitcase is the right panel for a 12V battery, not for a power station. It is a complete charging kit for an RV house battery, a trolling motor battery or a van build, with the charge controller already mounted on the back.

**Built-in controller, direct to battery.** Two rigid 50W panels hinge together in an aluminum frame, and a charge controller on the back connects to your battery with alligator clips. Renogy's controllers support common chemistries, including lithium on current versions, so it can top up an AGM or [LiFePO4](/glossary/lifepo4/) battery without extra parts. Check the listing for the controller model and its settings.

**Why it is the wrong choice for a power station.** Every portable station already has its own [MPPT](/glossary/mppt/) controller, so the suitcase's controller sits in the way. A fabric folding panel like the [Jackery SolarSaga 100W](/gear/jackery-solarsaga-100w-solar-panel/) or [Anker SOLIX PS100](/gear/anker-solix-ps100-portable-solar-panel/) is lighter and plugs in directly.

**Size the harvest.** On a sunny summer day, 100W × 5 sun hours × 0.75 is about 375Wh, or roughly 30Ah into a 12V battery. That replaces a night of LED lights, a water pump and phone charging in a typical RV. Rigid glass and fold-out legs make it tougher than fabric, at the cost of weight and storage space.

Owners like the all-in-one setup and the sturdy frame. The common complaints are weight and the basic PWM controller on some versions. It is in the [best portable solar panel](/best-portable-solar-panel/) roundup as the pick for 12V batteries and RVs.

name: Goal Zero Boulder 100 Briefcase
amazonQuery: Goal Zero Boulder 100 Briefcase solar panel
summary: Goal Zero’s rigid 100W tempered-glass briefcase panel with a kickstand and APP output; the tough, chainable choice for Yeti owners who are hard on gear.
verdict:
The Goal Zero Boulder 100 Briefcase is the panel for people who are hard on gear. It trades weight and cost for a rigid build that survives truck beds, job sites and a garage where things get knocked over.

**Glass and aluminum, not fabric.** Goal Zero builds it from two 50W monocrystalline panels under tempered glass in an aluminum frame, hinged into a briefcase with a handle and an integrated kickstand. A fabric folder can tear or crease; this cannot, short of a hard hit on the glass. The cost is heft: it is much heavier than a fabric 100W panel and takes more room to store.

**Made for Goal Zero Yetis.** Output is an Anderson Powerpole (APP) connector, the solar input on Goal Zero's Yeti stations such as the [Yeti 1500X](/gear/goal-zero-yeti-1500x/). Boulders are designed to chain together for more input. Other brands need an APP adapter cable.

**Do the math before you chain.** On a clear summer day, 100W × 5 sun hours × 0.75 is about 375Wh. A Yeti 1500X holds 1,516Wh, so one panel needs about four of those days, and real outage use calls for two to four Boulders. The [power station runtime calculator](/tools/power-station-runtime-calculator/) shows what 375Wh a day will run.

Owners praise the toughness and the kickstand. The main complaints are weight and price per watt compared with folding panels. It is in our [best portable solar panel](/best-portable-solar-panel/) roundup as the most durable pick.

name: Goal Zero Nomad 20
summary: A 20W folding panel with a built-in kickstand, USB and 8mm outputs; it charges phones and power banks and grows into Goal Zero’s Sherpa banks and small Yetis.
verdict:
The Goal Zero Nomad 20 is a phone-and-power-bank panel that stands up on its own, and it grows into a small Goal Zero system if you add a Sherpa bank or a small Yeti later.

**The kickstand is the feature.** Most fabric USB panels have to be hung from a pack or propped against a rock. The Nomad 20 has an integrated kickstand, so you can aim it at the sun on a tailgate or a deck rail. A panel facing the sun squarely makes far more than one lying flat, especially in winter.

**Two outputs, two jobs.** A USB-A port charges a phone or power bank directly, and an 8mm port feeds Goal Zero's Sherpa power banks, such as the [Sherpa 100AC](/gear/goal-zero-sherpa-100ac/), and small Yeti stations. Nomads can also chain together for more input.

**Expect about half the rating.** A 20W rating describes ideal lab light. Through a 5V USB port, after heat and angle losses, real output in good sun often lands near 8–12W. Over 5 good sun hours that is roughly 40–60Wh, enough to fill a 10,000mAh bank (about 36Wh) and start on a second. Charge a bank rather than your phone, so passing clouds do not interrupt charging.

Owners like the sturdy build and how easy it is to aim. The common complaints are price per watt and weight compared with a [BigBlue 28W](/gear/bigblue-28w-solar-charger/) folder. It features in our [best solar power bank](/best-solar-power-bank/) roundup; for power station charging, step up to a 100W panel like the [Jackery SolarSaga 100W](/gear/jackery-solarsaga-100w-solar-panel/).

name: Jackery SolarSaga 200W
summary: Jackery’s 200W folding panel with kickstands and a DC8020 plug; the right size to refill a 1kWh Jackery Explorer in about a day and a half of sun.
verdict:
The Jackery SolarSaga 200W is the panel to pair with a mid-size or large Jackery Explorer. It doubles the harvest of the SolarSaga 100W while keeping Jackery's plug-and-play cabling.

**Sized for 1kWh-plus stations.** On a clear summer day with about 5 peak sun hours, 200W × 5 × 0.75 is roughly 750Wh. That puts back most of the 1,070Wh in a [Jackery Explorer 1000 v2](/gear/jackery-explorer-1000-v2/) in one day, which a single 100W panel cannot do. For an [Explorer 2000 v2](/gear/jackery-explorer-2000-v2/), plan on two.

**Jackery cabling, with adapters for others.** Output is Jackery's DC8020 plug, which fits current Explorer inputs directly. Other stations need an adapter cable, so if you own an EcoFlow or BLUETTI station, an MC4 panel like the [BLUETTI PV200](/gear/bluetti-pv200-solar-panel/) is the simpler buy. Built-in kickstands let you tilt it toward the sun, the cheapest way to add output.

**Bigger means heavier.** It folds for carrying but is noticeably larger and heavier than the 100W version. For one person carrying it to a backyard, that is fine. For a long walk to a campsite, two 100W panels split the load.

Owners like how simply it connects to an Explorer and how much it adds over a 100W panel. The main complaint is price per watt against generic MC4 panels. name: EcoFlow 160W Portable Solar Panel
summary: A mid-size 160W folding panel with MC4 output, a 21.4V rating and a kickstand case; light enough to carry one-handed and compatible with nearly every portable station.
verdict:
The EcoFlow 160W is the mid-size folding panel that fits most portable power stations: big enough to refill a River-class station in a day, light enough to carry one-handed.

**Right-sized for small and mid stations.** On a clear summer day with about 5 peak sun hours, 160W × 5 × 0.75 is roughly 600Wh. That fully refills a small station like the [EcoFlow River 3](/gear/ecoflow-river-3/) and puts back a good share of a 1kWh [Delta 3 Plus](/gear/ecoflow-delta-3-plus/). The [power station runtime calculator](/tools/power-station-runtime-calculator/) shows what 600Wh a day keeps running.

**Low voltage, wide compatibility.** EcoFlow lists 21.4V open-circuit, the same class as most 100W panels, so it sits inside the solar input range of nearly every portable station, including small ones that cannot take the [EcoFlow 400W](/gear/ecoflow-400w-portable-solar-panel/) panel's 48V. Output is MC4, with an XT60 cable for EcoFlow stations.

**The case is the stand.** Like EcoFlow's larger panels, the protective case folds out into a kickstand. At 15.4 lb it is about three-quarters the weight of the 220W Bifacial, which is the main reason to choose it over that panel.

Owners like the easy setup and the protective case. The main complaint is that the 220W Bifacial adds meaningfully more output for a modest step up in size. Compare it with the picks in our [best portable solar panel](/best-portable-solar-panel/) roundup and the [best EcoFlow power station](/best-ecoflow-power-station/) guide.

faqs.q: Can the EcoFlow 160W panel charge a River 3?
faqs.a: Yes. Its 21.4V open-circuit voltage sits inside the River 3’s solar input range, and EcoFlow supplies an MC4-to-XT60 cable. The River 3 caps solar input below the panel’s 160W rating, so you will not see full output, but a sunny day still refills its 245Wh battery with room to spare.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the EcoFlow 160W and the EcoFlow 220W Bifacial?
faqs.a: Output, weight and the bifacial rear. The 220W harvests roughly 825Wh on a clear summer day versus about 600Wh, and its rear side can add more over reflective ground. The 160W weighs 15.4 lb versus 20.9 lb. Both use MC4 and similar voltages, so both fit most stations.
